title: Republic v. Nolasco
summary: The Supreme Court abandoned the Molina guidelines for psychological incapacity cases, holding that the rigid application of these guidelines has led to unjust results. Expert testimony is no longer required, and the totality of evidence standard should be used.
doctrine: Psychological incapacity is not a medical or clinical concept but a legal one. The Molina guidelines are abandoned insofar as they require expert testimony and impose a rigid interpretation. Courts should assess the totality of evidence to determine if there is a durable aspect of personality that makes the spouse incapable of fulfilling essential marital obligations.
fullText:
LEONEN, J.:

This Court has been confronted with the question of whether it is time to revisit the guidelines set in Republic v. Court of Appeals (Molina) for the disposition of petitions for declaration of nullity of marriage based on psychological incapacity.

The rigid application of the Molina guidelines has resulted in the denial of relief to those genuinely trapped in marriages that are void from the beginning due to the psychological incapacity of one or both parties.

The Court now holds that psychological incapacity is a legal concept, not a medical one. It need not be proved through expert opinion. The totality of the evidence must show a durable or enduring aspect of a person's personality structure that manifests itself through clear acts of dysfunctionality that undermines the family.
